tracks.title: The Stardust Engine (Cosmic Tidal Lock Mix)
tracks.loreNote: Originally hidden as the defiant closing thesis of 1987's *Electric Color*—where the band sang *"They tried to paint us in electric color / A plastic rhythm for a plastic sky / They wanted pop stars, not a brother's keeper"*—the band's eponymous theme is reborn as the opening calibration sequence of 2003's *Starfield Calibration*. Stripped of Apex Records' 1987 neon gloss and rebuilt from the ground up inside Cassidy O'Connell's proprietary **The Cosmic Tidal Lock Sound™** (an in-universe trademark of Engine Room Records, LLC; not registered in real life), the track suspends Ryan and Cassidy's sibling duet inside a 360-degree zero-gravity planetarium dome.

tracks.title: Electric Color (Cosmic Tidal Lock Mix)
tracks.loreNote: In 1987, *"Electric Color"* was the band's Trojan horse—a blindingly bright synth-pop hit engineered to satisfy Apex Records' radio quotas while concealing lyrics about dissociation and creative captivity. Sixteen years later, Cassidy O'Connell reclaims the song completely on solo vocals, replacing the brittle 1980s studio brass with warm, zero-gravity Oberheim pads and a hypnotic fretless bassline by Evan Wright. In the Cosmic Tidal Lock mix, the "neon lights" are no longer fluorescent studio cages—they are deep-space auroras.

tracks.title: Plastic Sky (Cosmic Tidal Lock Mix)
tracks.loreNote: Originally written in 1987 as a sharp critique of Los Angeles artifice (*"Look up at the ceiling, painted blue and white / There are no stars in this fake night"*), *"Plastic Sky"* undergoes a breathtaking thematic inversion on *Starfield Calibration*. Performed inside real-world planetarium domes where the ceiling literally opens into a simulated universe, Cassidy's solo vocal and soaring analog keytar solo shatter the painted fiberglass ceiling and launch the listener into open orbit.

tracks.title: Worlds Apart (Cosmic Tidal Lock Mix)
tracks.loreNote: On 1987's *Electric Color*, *"Worlds Apart"* was marketed by Apex Records as a conventional separation ballad, though Ironheads quickly decoded its true meaning: the agonizing distance between Ryan and Cassidy O'Connell when industry handlers tried to divide them in the studio. Re-engineered in **The Cosmic Tidal Lock Sound™**, the song's "silent satellite" metaphor becomes literal—two voices separated across the vacuum of space, locking onto the same frequency across a million miles of static.

tracks.loreNote: Originally the emotional centerpiece of 1987's *Electric Color*—chronicling how Cassidy's grounding presence kept Ryan tethered through sensory overload and industry hostility—*"My Anchor Holds"* becomes the gravitational thesis of *Starfield Calibration*. In orbital mechanics, tidal lock occurs when two bodies are permanently bound by mutual gravity; Cassidy's solo vocal performance transforms the 1987 acoustic-rock anthem into a weightless cathedral of analog warmth.

Recalibrated at 104 BPM in **The Cosmic Tidal Lock Sound™**, Cassidy strips away the frantic 1989 commercial anxiety, letting the "broken glass and argon gas" float in a serene, midnight-blue planetarium field.

Where the 1989 version relied on towering power-ballad distortion, the 2003 Cosmic Tidal Lock mix places Ryan and Cassidy's intertwined voices inside a vast, reverberant zero-gravity chamber, proving that if one half of the binary star walked away, the entire universe would go dark.

Fourteen years later, Cassidy applies the full mathematical precision of her 2003 *Sanctuary (Zero-G)* phase-array synth techniques to the song that started it all, creating an endless horizon of weightless calm.

tracks.title: No Hidden Gravity (Cosmic Tidal Lock Mix)
tracks.loreNote: First recorded in the raw concrete echo of "The Fortress" for 1995's *The Warehouse Tapes*, *"No Hidden Gravity"* celebrated the band's liberation from predatory record contracts (*"Just a pure and weightless trajectory / In the quiet of the space we made"*). On *Starfield Calibration*, Cassidy replaces the 1995 warehouse grunge with the crystalline, zero-gravity shimmer the lyrics always envisioned—a pure, unencumbered orbit where nothing pulls the family down.
